From fe2f8ad6f0999db3b318359a01ee0108c703a8c3 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: David Jeffery <djeffery@redhat.com>
Date: Tue, 13 Jan 2026 11:08:13 -0500
Subject: [PATCH] scsi: core: Wake up the error handler when final completions
 race against each other

The fragile ordering between marking commands completed or failed so
that the error handler only wakes when the last running command
completes or times out has race conditions. These race conditions can
cause the SCSI layer to fail to wake the error handler, leaving I/O
through the SCSI host stuck as the error state cannot advance.

First, there is an memory ordering issue within scsi_dec_host_busy().
The write which clears SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT may be reordered with reads
counting in scsi_host_busy(). While the local CPU will see its own
write, reordering can allow other CPUs in scsi_dec_host_busy() or
scsi_eh_inc_host_failed() to see a raised busy count, causing no CPU to
see a host busy equal to the host_failed count.

This race condition can be prevented with a memory barrier on the error
path to force the write to be visible before counting host busy
commands.

Second, there is a general ordering issue with scsi_eh_inc_host_failed(). By
counting busy commands before incrementing host_failed, it can race with a
final command in scsi_dec_host_busy(), such that scsi_dec_host_busy() does
not see host_failed incremented but scsi_eh_inc_host_failed() counts busy
commands before SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT is cleared by scsi_dec_host_busy(),
resulting in neither waking the error handler task.

This needs the call to scsi_host_busy() to be moved after host_failed is
incremented to close the race condition.

Fixes: 6eb045e092ef ("scsi: core: avoid host-wide host_busy counter for scsi_mq")
Signed-off-by: David Jeffery <djeffery@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Bart Van Assche <bvanassche@acm.org>
Link: https://patch.msgid.link/20260113161036.6730-1-djeffery@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>

diff --git a/drivers/scsi/scsi_lib.c b/drivers/scsi/scsi_lib.c
index c7d6b76c86d2..4a902c9dfd8b 100644
--- a/drivers/scsi/scsi_lib.c
+++ b/drivers/scsi/scsi_lib.c
@@ -376,6 +376,14 @@ static void scsi_dec_host_busy(struct Scsi_Host *shost, struct scsi_cmnd *cmd)
 	rcu_read_lock();
 	__clear_bit(SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT, &cmd->state);
 	if (unlikely(scsi_host_in_recovery(shost))) {
+		/*
+		 * Ensure the clear of SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT is visible to
+		 * other CPUs before counting busy requests. Otherwise,
+		 * reordering can cause CPUs to race and miss an eh wakeup
+		 * when no CPU sees all busy requests as done or timed out.
+		 */
+		smp_mb();
+
 		unsigned int busy = scsi_host_busy(shost);
 
 		spin_lock_irqsave(shost->host_lock, flags);
-- 
2.34.1



diff --git a/drivers/scsi/scsi_error.c b/drivers/scsi/scsi_error.c
index eebca96c1fc1..b6e8730e049e 100644
--- a/drivers/scsi/scsi_error.c
+++ b/drivers/scsi/scsi_error.c
@@ -282,11 +282,20 @@ static void scsi_eh_inc_host_failed(struct rcu_head *head)
 {
 	struct scsi_cmnd *scmd = container_of(head, typeof(*scmd), rcu);
 	struct Scsi_Host *shost = scmd->device->host;
-	unsigned int busy = scsi_host_busy(shost);
+	unsigned int busy;
 	unsigned long flags;
 
 	spin_lock_irqsave(shost->host_lock, flags);
 	shost->host_failed++;
+	spin_unlock_irqrestore(shost->host_lock, flags);
+	/*
+	 * The counting of busy requests needs to occur after adding to
+	 * host_failed or after the lock acquire for adding to host_failed
+	 * to prevent a race with host unbusy and missing an eh wakeup.
+	 */
+	busy = scsi_host_busy(shost);
+
+	spin_lock_irqsave(shost->host_lock, flags);
 	scsi_eh_wakeup(shost, busy);
 	spin_unlock_irqrestore(shost->host_lock, flags);
 }

## Summary of the Patch

The patch fixes two race conditions in the SCSI core that can prevent the error handler from being woken up when commands complete or time out concurrently. Both modifications ensure that the error handler is correctly notified when the number of busy commands equals the number of failed commands.

### Modifications in Each File

1. **`drivers/scsi/scsi_lib.c` – `scsi_dec_host_busy()`**  
   - Added a `smp_mb()` memory barrier after clearing the `SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT` bit and before calling `scsi_host_busy()` when the host is in recovery.  
   - This prevents memory reordering on other CPUs that could cause them to see an outdated `SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT` clear while still observing a higher `host_busy` count, thereby missing the condition to wake the error handler.

2. **`drivers/scsi/scsi_error.c` – `scsi_eh_inc_host_failed()`**  
   - Reordered the logic: `host_failed` is incremented *first* (while holding the host lock), then the lock is released, and only afterward is `scsi_host_busy()` called.  
   - Previously, `scsi_host_busy()` was called before incrementing `host_failed`, which could race with `scsi_dec_host_busy()`: the decrement might see `host_failed` not yet incremented, while the increment logic might have already read a busy count that does not yet reflect the clear of `SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT`. The new ordering ensures that `host_failed` is updated before counting busy commands, closing the window for a missed wakeup.

### Relationship Between Changes

Both changes target the same fundamental race: the error handler relies on comparing `host_busy` and `host_failed` to decide whether to wake up. The two endpoints of a command’s lifecycle—completion (in `scsi_dec_host_busy`) and failure/timeout (in `scsi_eh_inc_host_failed`)—must see consistent snapshots of both counters.  

- The memory barrier in `scsi_dec_host_busy` ensures visibility on the completion side.  
- The reordering in `scsi_eh_inc_host_failed` ensures that the busy count is taken after the failure count is updated, eliminating the opposite ordering race.  

Together, they guarantee that whichever path runs last will correctly observe that `host_busy == host_failed` and wake the error handler, thus preventing I/O from becoming stuck in the recovery state.

### Summary of Modifications

#### File: `drivers/scsi/scsi_error.c`
- **Function `scsi_eh_inc_host_failed()`**:
  - Reordered operations to increment `host_failed` before counting busy commands (`scsi_host_busy()`).
  - Previously: counted busy, then incremented `host_failed`, then called `scsi_eh_wakeup()`.
  - Now: increments `host_failed` under spinlock, releases lock, counts busy, re-acquires lock, and then calls `scsi_eh_wakeup()`.
  - **Purpose**: Prevents a race where a final command completing in `scsi_dec_host_busy()` might not see the updated `host_failed`, leading to failure to wake the error handler.

#### File: `drivers/scsi/scsi_lib.c`
- **Function `scsi_dec_host_busy()`**:
  - Added a `smp_mb()` memory barrier after clearing `SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT` and before calling `scsi_host_busy()` when the host is in recovery.
  - **Purpose**: Ensures the clear of the inflight flag is visible to other CPUs before reading the busy count. This prevents a race where reordering could cause another CPU to see a stale inflight flag, leading to an incorrect busy count and a missed error handler wakeup.

### Relationships Between Modifications
Both changes address the same fundamental race condition: the fragile ordering between marking commands completed (clearing inflight flag, decrementing busy count) and incrementing `host_failed` (counting failed commands). The race manifests as the error handler never waking, causing I/O to stall.

- The change in **scsi_lib.c** fixes a **memory ordering** issue: the write that clears the inflight flag may be reordered with later reads of the busy count, causing another CPU to see a mismatched count.
- The change in **scsi_error.c** fixes a **logic ordering** issue: counting busy commands before incrementing `host_failed` allows a window where the final command sees no new failures and the error handler sees no completed commands.

Together, the two modifications ensure that at least one side (the error handler or the final command) correctly sees the state where all commands are either done or failed, guaranteeing the error handler is woken. They are complementary and necessary to close the race completely.

- **Function `scsi_eh_inc_host_failed`**: Reordered the operations to ensure that `host_failed` is incremented **before** calling `scsi_host_busy()`. - The update of the inflight flag (`SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT`) and the busy count in `scsi_dec_host_busy()`, and
- The update of `host_failed` and the busy count in `scsi_eh_inc_host_failed()`.

The fix in `scsi_lib.c` ensures that the cleared inflight flag is visible to other CPUs before reading `host_busy`. Together, they guarantee that the condition `scsi_host_busy(shost) == shost->host_failed` is correctly evaluated across all CPUs, allowing the error handler to be woken when the last command finishes or times out.

Here is the commit message:
scsi: core: Wake up the error handler when final completions
 race against each other

The fragile ordering between marking commands completed or failed so
that the error handler only wakes when the last running command
completes or times out has race conditions. These race conditions can
cause the SCSI layer to fail to wake the error handler, leaving I/O
through the SCSI host stuck as the error state cannot advance.

First, there is an memory ordering issue within scsi_dec_host_busy().
The write which clears SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT may be reordered with reads
counting in scsi_host_busy(). While the local CPU will see its own
write, reordering can allow other CPUs in scsi_dec_host_busy() or
scsi_eh_inc_host_failed() to see a raised busy count, causing no CPU to
see a host busy equal to the host_failed count.

This race condition can be prevented with a memory barrier on the error
path to force the write to be visible before counting host busy
commands.

Second, there is a general ordering issue with scsi_eh_inc_host_failed(). By
counting busy commands before incrementing host_failed, it can race with a
final command in scsi_dec_host_busy(), such that scsi_dec_host_busy() does
not see host_failed incremented but scsi_eh_inc_host_failed() counts busy
commands before SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT is cleared by scsi_dec_host_busy(),
resulting in neither waking the error handler task.

This needs the call to scsi_host_busy() to be moved after host_failed is
incremented to close the race condition.

Fixes: 6eb045e092ef ("scsi: core: avoid host-wide host_busy counter for scsi_mq")

Reviewed-by: Bart Van Assche <bvanassche@acm.org>
Link: https://patch.msgid.link/20260113161036.6730-1-djeffery@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>

Here is the patch:

 static void scsi_dec_host_busy(struct Scsi_Host *shost, struct scsi_cmnd *cmd)
 {
 	unsigned long flags;
 
 	rcu_read_lock();
 	__clear_bit(SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT, &cmd->state);
 	if (unlikely(scsi_host_in_recovery(shost))) {
+		/*
+		 * Ensure the clear of SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT is visible to
+		 * other CPUs before counting busy requests. Otherwise,
+		 * reordering can cause CPUs to race and miss an eh wakeup
+		 * when no CPU sees all busy requests as done or timed out.
+		 */
+		smp_mb();

 		unsigned int busy = scsi_host_busy(shost);
 
 		spin_lock_irqsave(shost->host_lock, flags);
 		if (shost->host_failed || shost->host_eh_scheduled)
 			scsi_eh_wakeup(shost, busy);
 		spin_unlock_irqrestore(shost->host_lock, flags);
 	}
 	rcu_read_unlock();
 }

Reason:
The bug arises from two race conditions. Second, an ordering issue in `scsi_eh_inc_host_failed()`: it reads the busy count *before* incrementing `host_failed`. This can race with a final completion in `scsi_dec_host_busy()` such that neither side observes the correct condition – `scsi_dec_host_busy()` sees `host_failed` not yet incremented, and `scsi_eh_inc_host_failed()` sees the busy count before the inflight flag is cleared. - `smp_mb();` inserted in `scsi_dec_host_busy()` after `__clear_bit(SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT, &cmd->state);` and before the call to `scsi_host_busy(shost)`.
- In `scsi_eh_inc_host_failed()`, reorder the operations so that `host_failed` is incremented *before* reading the busy count: i.e., `shost->host_failed++;` followed by `unsigned int busy = scsi_host_busy(shost);`.

Reason:
The memory barrier (`smp_mb()`) forces the clear of `SCMD_STATE_INFLIGHT` to be globally visible before the subsequent read of `scsi_host_busy()` on the error path. This eliminates the memory ordering race by ensuring that when a CPU reads the busy count, it sees the updated inflight status. Moving the increment of `host_failed` before the busy count read in `scsi_eh_inc_host_failed()` closes the second race: now the completion path in `scsi_dec_host_busy()` will see the incremented `host_failed` while the error‑handling path counts the busy commands after the inflight flag is cleared. Together, these changes ensure that at least one CPU will observe `host_busy == host_failed` and wake the error handler.
